prompt: How are the BO6 octahedra connected in an ideal cubic ABO3 perovskite?

options.why: Corner-sharing BO6 octahedra form the 3D perovskite framework with A cations in 12-fold cavities.

options.text: As isolated zero-dimensional molecules with no shared oxygen atoms
options.why: Perovskite octahedra share every vertex oxygen with an adjacent octahedron.

options.text: By sharing faces along every axis simultaneously
options.why: Ideal cubic perovskites are corner-sharing, not all-face-sharing.

prompt: Why does shrinking the A-site cation across the lanthanide series in RCuO3 often require a larger supercell than the 5-atom cubic cell?

options.text: Smaller A-site ions drive cooperative octahedral tilting, and alternating tilts need a cell with more than one octahedron
options.why: Neighbouring octahedra rotate in opposite senses, so the repeat unit holds at least two of them; the five-atom cell cannot represent the tilt.

options.text: VASP cannot simulate cells with fewer than 20 atoms
options.why: VASP handles 5-atom cells easily; the supercell is required by the physical tilting distortion.

options.text: Oxygen atoms become magnetic only in larger cells
options.why: The supercell enlargement here is driven by structural octahedral tilting.

hints: Think about what happens to BO6 octahedra when the A-site cavity is too large for a small R3+ ion.

options.text: 3 atoms
options.why: Count all three species: 1 A + 1 B + 3 O.

options.text: 12 atoms

prompt: What does a Goldschmidt tolerance factor t close to 1 indicate for an ABO3 oxide?

options.text: Good geometric packing compatibility with an undistorted cubic perovskite
options.why: At t = 1, the A-O and B-O ideal bond lengths match the cubic perovskite geometry.

options.text: Guaranteed thermodynamic stability against all competing phases
options.why: Tolerance factors are geometric heuristics and do not prove thermodynamic stability.

options.text: That the compound must be a metal
options.why: Tolerance factors describe ionic packing geometry, not electronic conductivity.

options.text: t increases

options.text: t remains unchanged

options.why: If r_B / r_X is too small, anions touch before enclosing the B cation stably in an octahedron.

options.text: The plane-wave cutoff ENCUT required in VASP

options.text: The magnetic ordering temperature

prompt: Why should tolerance-factor screening always be followed by DFT total-energy checks?

options.text: Geometric packing heuristics do not compute electronic energies or competing-phase decomposition
options.why: t, mu and tau use only radii; they contain no electronic energy and no competing phases, so a composition that passes can still be unstable or decompose.

options.text: Tolerance factors only apply to pure metals
options.why: Tolerance factors are specifically designed for ionic compounds like perovskites.

options.text: Shannon radii are always exact at finite temperature
options.why: Shannon radii are empirical averages from many crystals, and even exact radii would not give an energy; stability needs total-energy calculations.

hints: Compare a geometric descriptor with a total-energy calculation.

options.text: Atomic mass and melting point

options.text: VASP ENCUT and k-mesh

options.text: Copy the 4-coordinated radius without noting the change

prompt: For a fixed element and coordination number, how does the Shannon ionic radius typically change as oxidation state increases?

options.text: It decreases because higher positive charge pulls remaining electrons closer
options.why: At a higher charge the same nucleus holds fewer electrons, so the remaining shells are pulled in and the tabulated radius is smaller (compare Cu2+ and Cu3+ in Shannon).

options.text: It increases linearly with oxidation state
options.why: Higher cations are smaller, not larger.

options.text: It never depends on oxidation state
options.why: Oxidation state is one of the primary keys in Shannon's table.

options.text: It increases with higher coordination number
options.why: More surrounding ligands increase anion-anion repulsion and lengthen bond distances.

options.text: It decreases by half
options.why: Higher coordination numbers correspond to larger effective ionic radii.

options.text: It is strictly identical for every coordination number
options.why: That is why Shannon tabulates separate radii per coordination number.

prompt: After completing a variable-cell ISIF = 3 relaxation in VASP, what should you run before reading the final total energy?

options.text: Copy CONTCAR to POSCAR and run a static calculation (IBRION = -1, NSW = 0)
options.why: The plane-wave set of a relaxation belongs to its starting cell; a static run on the final cell rebuilds the basis so the energy matches ENCUT.

options.text: Lower ENCUT to 200 eV to speed up the last step
options.why: The cutoff must stay at the converged value; a lower ENCUT gives an energy that cannot be compared with the other runs.

options.text: Delete CHGCAR and stop without checking forces
options.why: You still need to check that the forces met EDIFFG, and the static run must write CHGCAR for the DOS and band runs.

hints: Recall why a single ISIF = 3 run keeps its initial plane-wave basis.
Which run on the relaxation page gives the energy that is reported?

options.text: XDATCAR
options.why: XDATCAR stores ionic trajectory coordinates, not electron density.

options.text: OSZICAR

prompt: Why does a line-mode band-structure calculation use ISMEAR = 0 instead of ISMEAR = -5?

options.text: The tetrahedron method (ISMEAR = -5) requires a 3D k-mesh and cannot integrate along 1D band paths
options.why: Line-mode KPOINTS sample 1D segments, where tetrahedra are undefined.

options.text: ISMEAR = -5 is only allowed for molecules in a box
options.why: ISMEAR = -5 is for dense 3D k-meshes of solids, never for single Gamma-point molecules.

options.text: ISMEAR = 0 turns off spin polarization
options.why: Spin polarization is controlled by ISPIN, not ISMEAR.

options.why: The functional, the POTCARs, ENCUT and the k-point density all enter the total energy; mismatches shift raw energies by amounts far larger than the differences you want.

options.text: Only the job wall-time limit in the Slurm script
options.why: Wall-time limits do not change the physical Hamiltonian.

options.text: Only the comment line on line 1 of POSCAR

prompt: The structure page applies U to Cu 3d in LaCuO3. How should the value of U be chosen?

options.text: Scan a range (or compute U by linear response) and report how the results change
options.why: The common Materials Project list quoted in the protocol has no Cu value, so U must be scanned or computed, and conclusions shown across the range.

options.text: Copy U = 4 from the example INCAR, since it is the recommended value

options.text: Pick the value that opens the band gap you expect
options.why: Tuning U to an expected gap fits the model to a guess, and LaCuO3 is reported to be metallic, so this would go against experiment.

prompt: Cu3+ is 3d8. Why does the structure page start LaCuO3 three ways (non-magnetic, MAGMOM 3 on Cu, MAGMOM 1 on Cu)?

options.text: The SCF can land in different spin solutions depending on the start, and both high-spin and low-spin d8 are possible, so each start is tried and the energies compared
options.why: In an octahedron d8 nominally has two unpaired eg electrons, but a distortion or strong Cu-O covalency can favour a smaller moment; the start decides which local minimum the SCF finds.

options.text: MAGMOM fixes the final moment, so the three runs give three exact moments
options.why: MAGMOM is only the starting guess; the moment relaxes during the SCF and must be read from OUTCAR.

options.text: VASP needs three runs before ISPIN = 2 is allowed
options.why: There is no such rule; one spin-polarized run is enough to run, but not enough to be sure you found the lowest state.

hints: Draw the t2g and eg levels with eight electrons.
Is MAGMOM an input guess or a constraint?

visual.alt: Two ladders of five levels, spin up with five arrows and spin down with three, leaving two unpaired electrons.

prompt: In the ENCUT series for LaCuO3, what is held fixed between runs?

options.text: The cell, the k-mesh, the POTCARs and the spin start, in static runs; only ENCUT changes
options.why: Changing one setting at a time means every change in energy has one cause; static runs on the unrelaxed cell avoid adding geometry changes.

options.text: Nothing: the k-mesh is raised together with ENCUT to keep the cost balanced
options.why: If both change you cannot tell which one moved the energy.

options.text: Only the POTCARs; each run relaxes the cell at its own cutoff
options.why: Relaxing adds a second change (and Pulay stress) to every point; the protocol uses static runs on the same structure.

hints: How would you tell which setting caused a change in energy?
Look at NSW in the series INCAR.

visual.caption: Change in energy per atom from each cutoff to the next. Illustrative numbers.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy from one setting to the next on a logarithmic axis, falling below a dashed threshold line.

prompt: Why can the k-mesh series for LaCuO3 oscillate before it settles, while an insulator usually converges smoothly?

options.text: The compound is reported metallic, and each mesh samples the Fermi surface differently, so the occupied states change from mesh to mesh
options.why: In a metal, bands cross the Fermi level and the occupations depend on where the k-points fall; smearing softens this but a coarse mesh still jumps.

options.text: More k-points always lower the energy, just as more plane waves do
options.why: The variational argument applies to the basis set, not to Brillouin-zone sampling; k-mesh energies can go up or down.

options.text: Oscillation means ENCUT is too low
options.why: ENCUT is fixed during the k-mesh series; the oscillation comes from the zone integration.

hints: What is special about a metal at the Fermi level?
Does the variational principle say anything about k-point sampling?

visual.alt: Square reciprocal cell with a grid of dots for the k-points and a circle marking the Gamma point at the centre.

prompt: The Convergence Plotter accepts a series as converged at setting x_i when which condition holds?

options.text: Every later point stays within the tolerance of the energy per atom at x_i
options.why: The rule is the absolute value of (e_j - e_i) at or below the tolerance for all j > i, which a single flat stretch cannot fool.

options.text: The next point alone is within the tolerance
options.why: Two neighbouring points can agree by chance, especially in a metal; later points can still move.

options.text: The total energy matches the experimental cohesive energy
options.why: A total energy has no direct experimental counterpart; convergence is about how much it still changes with the setting.

hints: Why is "the next point is close" not enough?
The page writes the rule with "for all j > i".

visual.caption: A series with a flat stretch before a later jump. Illustrative numbers.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in energy from one setting to the next that dips below the threshold once, rises above it, then falls below it for good.

prompt: Why does the convergence page also converge the difference between the ferromagnetic and non-magnetic energies, not only the total energy?

options.text: It is the number the study reports, and errors common to both states cancel, so it may converge at a lower setting; that has to be checked, not assumed
options.why: Cancellation works only with the same cell, cutoff, mesh and POTCARs; testing the difference itself shows whether it has settled.

options.text: Energy differences never need testing because all errors cancel
options.why: Only errors that are the same for both states cancel; a difference can still change sign with an unconverged mesh in a metal.

options.text: The difference converges only if the two states use different k-meshes
options.why: Different meshes add an error to the difference instead of cancelling one.

hints: Which number does the project actually care about?
When do errors cancel between two calculations?

visual.caption: Change in an energy difference per formula unit from each setting to the next. Illustrative numbers.
visual.alt: Curve of the change in an energy difference from one setting to the next on a logarithmic axis, falling below a dashed threshold line.

prompt: The energy test passes at a cutoff below 1.3 times ENMAX. Why does the relaxation still use at least 1.3 times ENMAX?

options.text: The stress converges more slowly with the cutoff than the energy (Pulay stress), and a variable-cell relaxation is driven by the stress
options.why: With too few plane waves the stress is biased, so ISIF = 3 finds the wrong volume even when the energy looks converged.

options.text: VASP refuses to run below 1.3 times ENMAX
options.why: VASP runs at lower cutoffs; the 1.3 factor is a protocol rule for reliable stress.

options.text: A higher cutoff makes the SCF converge in fewer steps
options.why: More plane waves make each step more expensive and do not speed up convergence; the reason is the stress.

hints: Which quantity moves the cell in ISIF = 3?
Francis and Payne named the effect.

visual.caption: The number of plane waves grows with the cutoff.
visual.alt: Curve of the number of plane waves in the basis against the cutoff energy, rising faster than a straight line.

prompt: You relax the ten-atom LaCuO3 cell starting exactly from the ideal cubic positions, and it stays cubic. What can you conclude?

options.text: Nothing yet about the tilt: symmetry makes the tilt forces zero, so displace the oxygen atoms in the tilt pattern and relax again
options.why: At the cubic positions the forces that would start a rotation vanish by symmetry, so the relaxation cannot leave them even if a tilted structure is lower.

options.text: The cubic structure is the ground state in this model
options.why: A run that cannot move away from a symmetric point says nothing about whether that point is a minimum.

options.text: The ionic optimizer failed and IBRION must be changed
options.why: The optimizer did its job: the forces were already zero. Changing it does not break the symmetry.

hints: What are the forces on the oxygen atoms at the ideal positions?

prompt: Why is the energy of the last step of an ISIF = 3 relaxation unreliable after a large volume change?

options.text: The plane-wave set was built for the starting cell, so at the new volume the basis no longer matches ENCUT
options.why: VASP keeps the basis of the first step during the run; re-relaxing from CONTCAR and a static run on the final cell fix this.

options.text: VASP regenerates the k-mesh at every ionic step
options.why: The k-mesh in reciprocal coordinates stays the same during the run; the problem is the plane-wave basis.

options.text: MAGMOM is reset to its input value at every ionic step
options.why: The moments carry over from step to step; MAGMOM is only used at the start.

prompt: What does EDIFFG = -0.005 in the LaCuO3 relaxation INCAR mean?

options.text: Stop when every force is below 0.005 eV per angstrom
options.why: A negative EDIFFG sets a force criterion: the run stops when the largest force falls below its absolute value.

options.text: Stop when the total energy changes by less than 0.005 eV between ionic steps
options.why: That is what a positive EDIFFG means; the sign switches between an energy and a force criterion.

options.text: Stop when the stress is below 0.005 kB
options.why: EDIFFG does not set a stress threshold; with ISIF = 3 the stress is relaxed together with the forces, and you check the final pressure yourself.

hints: What does the minus sign switch?
The relaxation page writes the criterion with an absolute value.

prompt: Which comparison is sound for deciding whether G-type antiferromagnetic or ferromagnetic order is lower in LaCuO3?

options.text: Relax both in the same ten-atom cell, run a static SCF for each, compare energies per formula unit and check that the moments kept their pattern
options.why: The same cell cancels k-point and basis errors, static runs give clean energies, and the moment check confirms each energy belongs to the state it is named after.

options.text: Take the ferromagnetic energy from the five-atom cell and the G-type energy from the ten-atom cell, per atom
options.why: Different cells carry different k-point and basis errors, which can be as large as the difference.

options.text: Compare the energies of the first SCF before any relaxation
options.why: Each state can have its own relaxed volume; comparing unrelaxed energies ignores that.

prompt: With LORBIT = 11, what does the projected DOS show that the total DOS cannot?

options.text: Which orbitals carry the states near the Fermi level, for example Cu eg against O p
options.why: The projections weight each state by its overlap with spherical harmonics inside the sphere around each atom, which gives orbital character.

options.text: The exact number of electrons on each atom, because the projections add up to the total DOS
options.why: The spheres do not fill the cell, so the projections miss part of the density and do not sum to the total.

options.text: The measured photoemission spectrum
options.why: Kohn-Sham states are not quasiparticle energies, and the projections add orbital character, not a spectrum.

prompt: Your PBE+U run of LaCuO3 shows a small gap that is absent at U = 0. How should you read it?

options.text: As a sign that this U may be too large for a compound reported to be metallic, so show the results across the U scan
options.why: Adding U pushes occupied and empty d states apart and can open a gap; for a reported metal that is a warning about the U value, not a prediction.

options.text: As proof that LaCuO3 is an insulator
options.why: The measured behaviour is metallic, and a gap that depends on an adjustable parameter cannot overturn that.

options.text: As the optical gap to compare directly with experiment
options.why: A Kohn-Sham gap is not an optical gap, and with or without U it is not measured the same way.

prompt: Why must LMAXMIX = 4 stay in the ICHARG = 11 band run of LaCuO3?

options.text: The band run reads the density from CHGCAR, and the on-site d components are written and read only up to LMAXMIX; with a smaller value they are dropped and the density changes
options.why: Products of two d orbitals contribute components up to l = 4; with the default the on-site part is cut, so the fixed density is not the converged one.

options.text: LMAXMIX sets the number of bands in the run
options.why: The number of bands is NBANDS; LMAXMIX controls the angular momentum kept in the on-site density.

options.text: LMAXMIX is only read during relaxations
options.why: It matters in every run that mixes or reads the density of d or f electrons, and the protocol names the ICHARG = 11 run explicitly.
